problem: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines are assembled from independently chosen components—a document parser, a chunking strategy, and an embedding model—whose joint interactions are rarely evaluated systematically, especially across structurally distinct regulatory documents (p.1).
methodology: The authors conducted a controlled factorial study using 3 parsers, 3 chunking strategies, and 5 dense embedding models, plus a sparse (BM25) baseline, evaluated against an 800-question benchmark across 4 Indian central-government regulatory documents (p.1, p.2). They fitted linear mixed-effects models with document-query-level random intercepts to the 72,000-row result set, performed Holm-corrected paired comparisons, and reported clustered bootstrap confidence intervals for all 54 unique configurations (p.1).
dataset: An 800-question benchmark spread across four structurally distinct Indian central-government regulatory documents: Central Civil Services (Leave) Rules 1972, CCS (Conduct) Rules 1964, Fundamental Rules & Supplementary Rules Part I, and the Right to Information Act 2005 (p.1, p.3).
results: No single retriever family dominated across documents, with BM25 outperforming dense retrieval on some documents while the reverse held on others (p.1). The best overall configuration was normal parsing with advanced chunking and the BGE-small embedding, achieving an Evidence Recall@10 of 0.958 (p.6). MPNet-base significantly underperformed with a specific severe failure mode on table-derived questions (p.1, p.8).
key_findings: Parser and chunker choices interact significantly, and the best-performing combination is not predictable from individual component rankings (p.1). The corpus exhibited a near-saturated evidence-preservation ceiling (>98%) across all parsing/chunking combinations, demonstrating that retrieval differences are driven almost entirely by ranking quality rather than information loss during ingestion (p.1).
limitations: The study is restricted to four documents from a single domain (Indian central-government administrative/legal texts) (p.11). Question-evidence pairs were generated by an LLM with a 10% manual spot-check and de-duplication pass rather than being fully human-authored or evaluated for inter-annotator agreement (p.11). The evaluation is retrieval-only with no generation-stage evaluation, no cross-encoder reranking stage, and no hybrid sparse-dense baseline tested (p.11).
title: Parser, Chunking, and Embedding Interactions in Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Indian Government Regulatory Documents
